decks.title: Manufacturing Industries — Part 1: Importance and classification
goals: Explain how industries contribute to employment, exports and self-reliance
Classify industries by size, raw material and ownership
Weigh the factors that decide where an industry is located

slides.heading: From raw material to finished goods
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **manufacturing** turns raw materials into goods of higher value: cane into sugar, cotton into cloth, cocoons into silk sarees, iron ore into steel. It is the heart of the **secondary sector**.

visual.alt: Table of raw materials, the manufactured products made from them and an example centre

slides.narration: Namaste! Manufacturing means turning raw materials into finished goods that are worth more. Sugarcane becomes sugar, raw cotton becomes cloth, silk cocoons become sarees, and iron ore becomes steel. Manufacturing belongs to the secondary sector of the economy. In this part we see why it matters so much, how industries are classified, and what decides where a factory is built.

slides.heading: Importance of manufacturing: jobs and value
slides.body_md: **Employment:** factories, workshops and the services around them employ millions and draw surplus workers away from farming. **Value addition:** processing raises the value of raw materials many times. **Modernising agriculture:** industry supplies tractors, pumps, fertilisers and pesticides, and agro-based industries buy farm produce. **Balanced development:** new industries in backward regions bring roads, power, schools and towns.

nodes.label: Raw materials from farms and mines
Incomes rise; towns and services grow

visual.alt: Flow from raw materials to factories to value addition, jobs and growth

slides.narration: Why does manufacturing matter? It gives jobs to millions of people and takes pressure off farmland, where too many people already work. It adds value: a tonne of raw cotton becomes cloth worth many times more. It supports farming by making tractors, pumps and fertilisers, and by buying cane, cotton and silk. And new factories bring roads, power and towns to backward areas.

slides.heading: Importance of manufacturing: exports and self-reliance
slides.body_md: **Exports:** manufactured goods such as textiles, garments, steel, chemicals, medicines, vehicles and electronics earn **foreign exchange**, which pays for imports such as crude oil. **Self-reliance:** making our own machines, steel, fertilisers and defence equipment reduces **dependence on imports** and protects the country in emergencies. **Strength of the economy:** a strong manufacturing base raises national income and the standard of living.

rows: Textile mills and powerlooms of Surat
Sugar mills buying cane from farmers

visual.alt: Table of benefits of manufacturing with an example of each

slides.narration: Factories also earn money from abroad. Garments, cloth, steel, medicines and vehicles are sold to other countries, and the foreign exchange they earn pays for things we must import, such as crude oil. When we make our own machines, steel, fertilisers and defence goods, we depend less on other nations. So a strong manufacturing base makes the whole country stronger and more self reliant.

slides.heading: Classification by size
slides.body_md: **Large-scale industries** need huge **capital**, employ thousands of workers, use heavy machinery and produce in bulk — integrated steel plants, cotton mills, oil refineries, fertiliser plants. **Small-scale industries** need less capital and fewer workers, often use family labour and simple machines — handlooms, powerlooms, food processing, toys, sports goods. **Cottage industries** run in homes with traditional skills — pottery, handloom weaving, basket making. Small-scale units create many jobs for each rupee invested.

rows: A few to a few hundred

visual.alt: Table comparing large-scale and small-scale industries

slides.narration: Industries can be grouped by size. Large scale industries, like steel plants and big cotton mills, need huge amounts of money, thousands of workers and heavy machines. Small scale industries, like powerlooms, food processing and sports goods units, need less money and fewer workers. Cottage industries are run at home by families using traditional skills, such as pottery and handloom weaving.

slides.heading: Classification by raw material and by ownership
slides.body_md: **By raw material:** **agro-based** industries use farm produce — sugar, cotton textiles, jute, silk, vegetable oil, tea, food processing; **mineral-based** industries use minerals — iron and steel, aluminium, cement, petrochemicals; others are **forest-based** (paper, plywood) or **marine-based** (fish processing). **By ownership:** **public sector** — owned and run by the government (Steel Authority of India, BHEL); **private sector** — owned by individuals or companies (Tata Steel, Reliance Industries); **joint sector** — owned by the government and private firms together; **cooperative sector** — owned by the producers or workers who supply the raw material (sugar cooperatives of Maharashtra, Amul dairy at Anand).

visual.alt: Tree showing classification of industries by raw material and by ownership

slides.narration: Industries can also be grouped by the raw material they use. Agro based industries, such as sugar, cotton and silk, use farm produce. Mineral based industries, such as steel, cement and petrochemicals, use minerals. By ownership, public sector industries belong to the government, private sector firms to individuals or companies, joint sector firms to both, and cooperatives to the farmers or workers who supply them.

slides.heading: Worked example: classifying industries
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Classify each industry by raw material and by ownership.

**(a)** A cooperative sugar mill near Kolhapur owned by cane growers → **agro-based; cooperative sector**.

**(b)** The Bhilai steel plant of the Steel Authority of India → **mineral-based; public sector**.

**(c)** A family-owned silk-weaving unit in Kanchipuram → **agro-based; private sector, small-scale**.

**(d)** A company-owned petrochemical complex at Jamnagar → **mineral-based; private sector, large-scale**.

**Method.** Ask two questions: *Where does the raw material come from?* and *Who owns the unit?*

visual.alt: Table classifying four industries by raw material and ownership

slides.narration: To classify an industry, ask two questions. Where does its raw material come from, and who owns it? A sugar mill near Kolhapur owned by cane growers is agro based and cooperative. The Bhilai steel plant is mineral based and in the public sector. A family silk unit in Kanchipuram is agro based and private. A company owned petrochemical complex at Jamnagar is mineral based and private.

slides.heading: Factors of location
slides.body_md: An industry is located where its total costs are lowest. **Physical factors:** **raw material** (especially if bulky or perishable), **power**, **water**, **climate**. **Human and economic factors:** **labour** (cheap or skilled), **market**, **transport** (railways, roads, ports), **capital** and banking, **government policy** (incentives, industrial estates). Industries using **heavy, bulky or perishable** raw materials, such as sugar and steel, are pulled towards the raw material; industries making goods that are fragile or costly to carry are pulled towards the **market**.

visual.alt: Table of location factors and industries strongly pulled by each

slides.narration: Where should a factory be built? Owners look for the place where total costs are lowest. They think about raw material, power, water and climate, and also about workers, markets, transport, money and government support. If the raw material is heavy or spoils quickly, as with sugarcane, the factory goes near the raw material. If the product is costly to carry, it goes near the market.

slides.heading: Worked example: weighing the factors
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two sites are scored out of 10 for a new sugar mill (illustrative). Weights reflect each factor's importance for sugar: raw material 0.35, market 0.2, power 0.15, labour 0.15, transport 0.15. Which site should be chosen?

**Step 1.** Site P: 0.35 × 9 + 0.2 × 5 + 0.15 × 6 + 0.15 × 7 + 0.15 × 6 = **7**.

**Step 2.** Site Q: 0.35 × 4 + 0.2 × 9 + 0.15 × 8 + 0.15 × 7 + 0.15 × 8 = **6.65**.

**Step 3. Decide.** Site P wins, although Q scores higher on market, power and transport, because the heavily weighted factor — nearness to cane — matters most for a perishable, bulky raw material.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Manufacturing adds value, creates jobs, earns foreign exchange through exports, supports agriculture and builds self-reliance.
By size: large-scale (steel plants, cotton mills) and small-scale or cottage (powerlooms, handlooms, food processing).
By raw material: agro-based (sugar, cotton, silk) and mineral-based (steel, cement, petrochemicals).
By ownership: public, private, joint and cooperative sectors.
Location: raw material, power, water, climate, labour, market, transport, capital and policy.

visual.alt: Summary table of the bases of classification

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Manufacturing adds value, creates jobs, earns foreign exchange and makes the country self reliant. Industries are classified by size into large and small scale, by raw material into agro based and mineral based, and by ownership into public, private, joint and cooperative. Their location depends on raw material, power, labour, markets, transport and policy.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: For importance, give named examples: Tiruppur garments, Kolhapur sugar cooperatives.
Classify each industry on all three bases when asked.
Cooperatives are owned by the producers who supply the raw material.
For location, name the factor and explain how it lowers costs.

decks.title: Manufacturing Industries — Part 2: Sugar, cotton textiles and silk
goals: Explain why sugar mills are located close to sugarcane fields and why the industry has shifted to peninsular India
Explain the factors that favoured the cotton textile industry in Mumbai and Ahmedabad
Name the types of silk and the major silk centres, and explain why Karnataka leads in mulberry silk

slides.heading: Industries that begin on the farm
slides.body_md: Part 2 — three great agro-based industries: **sugar**, which must be close to its cane; **cotton textiles**, among the oldest modern industries of India; and **silk**, a craft and an industry that keeps millions of rural families busy.

visual.alt: Table of three agro-based industries with their raw material and leading regions

slides.narration: In this part we study three industries that begin on the farm. Sugar mills must stand close to the cane fields. Cotton textiles are among the oldest modern industries in India. And silk, from the cocoons of silkworms, supports millions of rural families. For each, we ask where it is found, why it is there, and what problems it faces.

slides.heading: Sugar: why mills stand among the cane fields
slides.body_md: Sugarcane is **heavy and bulky** — only about a tenth of its weight becomes sugar — so carrying it far is costly. It is also **perishable**: once cut, its **sucrose content starts falling**, so it must be crushed within about a day. It cannot be stored. So sugar mills are built **in the cane-growing belt**, and farmers bring cane by tractor or bullock cart within a short radius. Mills also need water, cheap labour in the crushing season, and transport for the finished sugar.

nodes.label: Cane is bulky; little of its weight becomes sugar
Mills built in the cane belt

visual.alt: Flow showing why bulky, perishable cane pulls sugar mills into the cane belt

slides.narration: Sugarcane is heavy and bulky, and only about a tenth of its weight ends up as sugar, so it is expensive to carry far. Worse, once the cane is cut, its sugar starts to break down, so it must be crushed within about a day. It cannot be stored. That is why sugar mills are built right among the cane fields, and farmers bring their cane in by tractor and bullock cart.

slides.heading: Delay costs sugar (illustrative)
slides.body_md: The illustrative graph shows sugar recovered from cane falling as crushing is delayed: 0 h — 11%; 24 h — 10.5%; 48 h — 9.8%; 72 h — 9%. A mill that keeps cane waiting loses sugar every hour, which is why mills schedule cutting and crushing together and buy cane only from nearby fields.

Every hour of delay costs sugar, so mills plan cutting and crushing together and take cane only from nearby fields.

slides.heading: Sugar: distribution and the shift to the peninsula
slides.body_md: **Distribution:** **Uttar Pradesh** and **Maharashtra** are the leading producers **(as of the early 2020s)**, followed by **Karnataka**, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Bihar and Andhra Pradesh. **Shift to peninsular India:** cane in the warmer south and west has a **higher sucrose content** and a **higher yield per hectare**; the frost-free tropical climate allows a **longer crushing season**; **cooperative mills** in Maharashtra are well managed and invest in modern machinery; newer, larger mills are more efficient than many old mills of the north; coastal and irrigated areas give steady cane supply.

visual.alt: Table comparing sugar production conditions in the northern plains and the peninsula

slides.narration: Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra are the leading sugar producing states, followed by Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Over the years the industry has grown faster in the peninsula. There, the warm, frost free climate gives cane with more sugar and a bigger harvest per hectare, and mills can crush for more months of the year. Maharashtra’s cooperative mills are also well run and modern.

slides.heading: Sugar: process, by-products and problems
slides.body_md: **Process:** cane is crushed to extract juice → juice is cleaned → boiled and concentrated → crystallised → separated in centrifuges → sugar. **By-products:** **bagasse** (fibre) is burnt as fuel or made into paper and boards; **molasses** is used to make **industrial alcohol (ethanol)**; **press mud** is used as manure. **Problems:** crushing is **seasonal** (a few months a year), so workers and machines sit idle; **low yield** and low sucrose in the north; **old, small mills**; high cost of production; delays in paying farmers; competition from **gur and khandsari** makers.

visual.alt: Flow of sugar making with by-products bagasse and molasses

slides.narration: In the mill, cane is crushed for its juice, which is cleaned, boiled and crystallised into sugar. Nothing is wasted: the fibre, called bagasse, is burnt as fuel or made into paper, molasses becomes industrial alcohol, and press mud becomes manure. But the industry has problems. It works only a few months a year, many northern mills are old and small, and costs are high.

slides.heading: Worked example: what does waiting cost?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Because of a transport strike, 2000 t of cane waits 72 hours before crushing instead of being crushed at once. Using the illustrative recoveries, how much sugar is lost?

**Step 1.** Crushed at once: $\frac{11}{100} \times 2000 = 220$ t of sugar.

**Step 2.** After 72 hours: $\frac{9}{100} \times 2000 = 180$ t.

**Step 3.** Loss $= 220 - 180 = 40$ t — lost to the mill and to the farmers, which is why mills are sited within easy reach of the fields.

visual.alt: Table of illustrative sugar obtained with no delay and after three days

slides.narration: Suppose two thousand tonnes of cane is held up for three days by a strike. Crushed at once, it would give two hundred and twenty tonnes of sugar. After three days it gives only one hundred and eighty. Forty tonnes of sugar are lost, a heavy blow to both the mill and the farmers. That is the cost of distance and delay for a perishable raw material.

slides.heading: Cotton textiles: why Mumbai and Ahmedabad
slides.body_md: **Mumbai** grew as the first great centre ("Cottonopolis of India"): **humid coastal climate** keeps yarn from breaking during spinning; a **port** to import machinery and export cloth; **capital** from merchants who had traded in raw cotton; raw cotton from the **black-soil cotton belt** of Maharashtra and Gujarat, brought by **railway**; **cheap labour** from the Konkan and Deccan; and **hydroelectric power** from the Western Ghats. **Ahmedabad** ("Manchester of India") had **cotton fields** of Gujarat around it, local merchant **capital**, cheap **labour**, a large **market**, a fairly humid climate, and access to ports.

rows: From the Deccan and Gujarat cotton belt

visual.alt: Table comparing the factors that favoured cotton mills in Mumbai and Ahmedabad

slides.narration: Why did cotton mills first grow in Mumbai? Its damp sea air stopped the yarn from snapping, its port brought in machines and sent out cloth, and its traders had money to invest. Railways carried raw cotton from the black soil belt, workers came from the Konkan, and hydro power came from the Western Ghats. Ahmedabad had cotton fields all around it, local capital, workers and a big market.

slides.heading: Quick check: cotton textiles
slides.body_md: Name a factor that favoured cotton mills in Mumbai or Ahmedabad.
slides.narration: Quick check. Humid air, a port, capital and the cotton belt favoured Mumbai.

slides.heading: Cotton textiles: other centres and problems
slides.body_md: **Other centres:** **Coimbatore** ("Manchester of South India") — cotton, cheap power and skilled labour; **Kanpur** in Uttar Pradesh; **Surat** (now mainly synthetic fabrics); Solapur, Nagpur, Indore, Madurai, Tiruppur (knitwear and garments), Kolkata. **Problems:** **old, obsolete machinery** in many mills; **power shortages** and high power cost; **competition from synthetic fibres** and from **powerlooms**; shortage of **long-staple cotton**, part of which is imported; low productivity; many **sick (loss-making) mills** closed in Mumbai; strong **foreign competition** in exports.

visual.alt: Table of problems of the cotton textile industry and their effects

slides.narration: Cotton mills later spread to Coimbatore, the Manchester of South India, and to Kanpur, Indore, Nagpur, Solapur and many other towns. Tiruppur makes knitwear for export. But the industry has problems: many mills have old machines, power is short or costly, synthetic fabrics and powerlooms take away buyers, and fine long staple cotton must partly be imported. Many old Mumbai mills have closed.

slides.heading: Worked example: why Ahmedabad overtook its rivals
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain why Ahmedabad became one of India’s largest cotton textile centres.

**Step 1. Raw material.** The black soils of Gujarat grow cotton close by, so raw cotton is cheap to bring in.

**Step 2. Capital and enterprise.** Local merchant families invested their trading profits in mills.

**Step 3. Labour and market.** Cheap labour from the surrounding villages; a large market in Gujarat, Rajasthan and beyond.

**Step 4. Transport and climate.** Rail links and nearby ports; a fairly humid climate in the mill season.

visual.alt: Flow of four factors that made Ahmedabad a great cotton textile centre

slides.narration: Why did Ahmedabad grow into a great textile city? Cotton grows on the black soils of Gujarat close by. Local merchant families put their trading profits into building mills. Workers came from the surrounding villages, and the cloth found buyers across western India. Railways and nearby ports carried cotton in and cloth out. No wonder it was called the Manchester of India.

slides.heading: Silk: from silkworm to thread
slides.body_md: Silk comes from the **cocoons** spun by silkworms. **Sericulture** is the rearing of silkworms. India produces all four commercial kinds of silk: **mulberry** (worms fed on mulberry leaves), **tasar** (on arjun, asan and sal; temperate tasar on oak), **eri** (on castor leaves) and **muga**, the golden silk found only in **Assam** (on som and soalu leaves). At **reeling** units, cocoons are boiled and the thread unwound; roughly 8 kg of cocoons give 1 kg of raw silk (illustrative).

Tasar comes from worms that eat arjun, asan or sal leaves. Eri worms feed on castor leaves, and golden muga silk is made only in Assam. Cocoons are boiled and unwound into thread; about eight kilograms of cocoons give one kilogram of raw silk.

slides.heading: Silk centres and Karnataka’s lead
slides.body_md: **Centres:** **Karnataka** — Bengaluru, Mysuru, **Ramanagara** (a huge cocoon market), Kolar, Chikkaballapur; **Kanchipuram** (Tamil Nadu) and **Dharmavaram** (Andhra Pradesh) for silk sarees; **Varanasi** for brocades; **Bhagalpur** (Bihar) for tasar; **Sualkuchi** (Assam) for muga and mulberry weaving; **Murshidabad** (West Bengal); Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh for tasar. **Why Karnataka leads in mulberry silk:** an **equable plateau climate** with moderate temperature all year lets mulberry grow continuously, so farmers rear **five or more crops** of cocoons a year; red loamy soils and irrigation suit mulberry; **traditional skills**; **government support**, research institutes and **organised cocoon markets**.

Other centres include Kanchipuram for sarees, Varanasi for brocades, Bhagalpur for tasar and Sualkuchi in Assam for muga.

notes.title: Manufacturing Industries: Classification and Agro-based Industries — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Importance of manufacturing industries
sections.body_md:
- **Manufacturing:** processing raw materials into goods of higher value (secondary sector).
- **Employment:** jobs in factories and related services; reduces pressure on agriculture.
- **Value addition** and higher national income.
- **Exports:** textiles, garments, steel, chemicals, medicines, vehicles, electronics earn foreign exchange.
- **Self-reliance:** home-made machinery, steel, fertilisers and defence goods reduce imports.
- **Support to agriculture:** tractors, pumps, fertilisers; agro-based industries buy farm produce.
- **Regional development:** industries bring infrastructure and towns to backward areas.

key_terms.definition_md: Converting raw materials into finished goods of higher value.
The increase in the worth of a material when it is processed into a product.

visual.alt: Table of benefits of manufacturing with examples

sections.heading: 2. Classification of industries
sections.body_md:
| Basis | Types | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Large-scale; small-scale; cottage | Steel plant; powerloom unit; handloom |
| Raw material | Agro-based; mineral-based; forest-based; marine-based | Sugar, cotton, silk; steel, cement, petrochemicals; paper; fish canning |
| Ownership | Public; private; joint; cooperative | SAIL, BHEL; Tata Steel, Reliance; government + private; Kolhapur sugar cooperatives, Amul |

- **Location factors:** raw material, power, water, climate, labour, market, transport, capital, government policy.
- Bulky or perishable raw materials pull industries towards their source; fragile or costly-to-carry products pull them towards markets.

key_terms.definition_md: An industry that uses farm produce as its raw material, such as sugar or cotton textiles.
Industries owned and run by the producers or workers who supply the raw material.
Industries owned and managed by the government.

visual.alt: Table of ownership sectors and their owners

sections.heading: 3. Sugar industry
sections.body_md:
- **Location near cane fields:** cane is heavy and bulky (only about a tenth becomes sugar); sucrose falls soon after cutting, so cane must be crushed within about a day; it cannot be stored.
- **Leading states (as of the early 2020s):** Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra; also Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh.
- **Shift to the peninsula:** higher sucrose content and yield per hectare; longer crushing season in a frost-free climate; well-run cooperatives in Maharashtra; newer, larger mills.
- **By-products:** bagasse (fuel, paper, boards); molasses (industrial alcohol, ethanol); press mud (manure).
- **Problems:** seasonal working; low yields and sucrose in the north; old, small mills; high costs; delayed payments to farmers; competition from gur and khandsari.

key_terms.definition_md: A thick syrup left after sugar crystals are removed, used to make industrial alcohol.
The months in which a sugar mill crushes cane.

visual.alt: Table comparing sugar production in the north and the peninsula

sections.heading: 4. Cotton textile industry
sections.body_md:
- **Mumbai:** humid coastal climate; port for machinery and exports; capital of cotton traders; raw cotton from the black-soil cotton belt by rail; cheap labour from the Konkan and Deccan; hydel power from the Western Ghats.
- **Ahmedabad (Manchester of India):** cotton fields of Gujarat nearby; local merchant capital; cheap labour; large market; ports and railways.
- **Other centres:** Coimbatore (Manchester of South India), Kanpur, Surat, Solapur, Nagpur, Indore, Madurai, Tiruppur, Kolkata.
- **Problems:** obsolete machinery; power shortage and cost; competition from synthetic fibres and powerlooms; shortage of long-staple cotton; low productivity; sick mills; foreign competition.

key_terms.definition_md: A name for Mumbai, the first great centre of cotton mills.
Cotton with long fibres, used for fine yarn and cloth.

visual.alt: Table of cotton textile centres and their nicknames or specialities

sections.heading: 5. Silk textile industry
sections.body_md:
- **Sericulture:** rearing silkworms for silk; cocoons are boiled and reeled into raw silk (roughly 8 kg of cocoons per kg of raw silk, illustrative).
- **Types:** mulberry (mulberry leaves; Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal); tasar (arjun, asan, sal; oak for temperate tasar; Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Bihar); eri (castor; Assam, Meghalaya); muga (golden; som and soalu; Assam only).
- **Centres:** Bengaluru, Mysuru, Ramanagara (cocoon market); Kanchipuram; Dharmavaram; Varanasi; Bhagalpur (tasar); Sualkuchi (Assam); Murshidabad.
- **Karnataka leads in mulberry silk:** equable plateau climate lets mulberry grow all year (five or more cocoon crops a year); suitable red loamy soils and irrigation; traditional skills; government support, research and organised cocoon markets.

key_terms.definition_md: The rearing of silkworms for the production of silk.
A golden silk produced only in Assam.

questions.stem_md: Garment factories in Tiruppur sell most of their knitwear to buyers in Europe and the USA. For India, the most direct benefit of this is that it:

options.text_md: reduces the need for cotton farming
earns foreign exchange that helps pay for imports such as crude oil

questions.solution_md: Exports bring in foreign exchange — option (c).

questions.stem_md: India once imported most of its fertilisers and much of its machinery. Building its own fertiliser and machine-tool plants mainly helped the country to:

options.text_md: become more self-reliant and save on imports

questions.solution_md: Home production reduces dependence on imports — option (c).

options.text_md: Farm output falls because land is no longer needed
Some surplus farm workers find jobs, and farmers get a nearby buyer for their produce

questions.solution_md: Manufacturing absorbs surplus labour and links with agriculture — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Agro-based industries help to raise farmers’ incomes.

**Reason (R):** Such industries buy farm produce such as cane, cotton and cocoons as their raw material.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Manufacturing belongs to the primary sector of the economy.
questions.solution_md: False: it belongs to the secondary sector.

questions.solution_md: **Secondary** sector.

questions.stem_md: Explain two ways in which the steel and fertiliser plants built after independence helped India become self-reliant.

answer.model_answer_md: They reduced the need to import steel and fertilisers, saving foreign exchange for other needs. They supplied home-made steel for railways, machines and defence, and fertilisers for the Green Revolution, so the country did not depend on other nations for these essentials.

questions.solution_md: Fewer imports; home supply of essentials.

questions.stem_md: Explain how manufacturing industries contribute to (a) employment, (b) exports and (c) the development of agriculture.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Factories, workshops and their transport and trade employ millions, taking surplus workers away from overcrowded farms. (b) Manufactured goods such as garments, steel, medicines and vehicles are sold abroad and earn foreign exchange. (c) Industry supplies tractors, pumps, fertilisers and pesticides, while agro-based industries buy cane, cotton and silk cocoons and so raise farmers’ incomes.

questions.solution_md: Employment; exports; links with agriculture.

questions.stem_md: A dairy in Anand is owned by thousands of milk producers who supply it and share its profits. On the basis of ownership it belongs to the:

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a small-scale industry?

options.text_md: An integrated steel plant at Rourkela
A large cotton mill complex with thousands of workers
A powerloom unit in Bhiwandi with a dozen looms and twenty workers

questions.stem_md: Which group lists only agro-based industries?

options.text_md: A sugar mill, because cane is bulky and spoils soon after cutting
A software company, because code is heavy
A jewellery workshop, because gold is bulky
A printing press, because paper spoils in a day

questions.solution_md: Bulky, perishable raw material → location at the source — option (a).

questions.solution_md: SAIL.

options.text_md: A cane growers’ sugar mill near Sangli

questions.stem_md: Classify (a) the Tata Steel works at Jamshedpur and (b) a cooperative sugar mill in Kolhapur on the basis of raw material and ownership.

questions.stem_md: Explain how (a) raw material, (b) market and (c) power influence the location of industries, with an Indian example of each.

questions.stem_md: A sugar mill near Gorakhpur, built about seventy years ago, makes losses although cane is grown all around it. State two problems of the sugar industry in the northern plains that probably explain this.

Cane yield per hectare and sucrose content are lower than in the south, and the crushing season is short, so mills stand idle for much of the year (also delayed payments to farmers, competition from gur and khandsari).

questions.solution_md: Old mills; low yield and short season.

questions.stem_md: A planner compares a cooperative sugar mill near Sangli in Maharashtra with an older mill near Gorakhpur in Uttar Pradesh. Explain three reasons why the Sangli mill is likely to be more productive.

answer.model_answer_md: Cane in the warm, frost-free peninsula has a higher sucrose content and a higher yield per hectare, so each tonne crushed gives more sugar. The crushing season is longer because cane can be harvested over more months, so machinery and workers are used for longer. Maharashtra’s cooperative mills are owned by the cane growers, are well managed and have invested in newer, larger machinery, while many northern mills are old and small.

questions.solution_md: Sucrose and yield; longer season; cooperative, modern mills.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Give two reasons why manufacturing industries are important for India. [2]

(b) Distinguish between agro-based and mineral-based industries, with one example of each. [2]

(c) Explain the classification of industries on the basis of ownership, giving an Indian example of each type. [3]

(d) Classify the following on all three bases (size, raw material, ownership): (i) the Rourkela steel plant, (ii) a family silk-weaving unit in Kanchipuram, (iii) a cane growers’ sugar mill near Kolhapur. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) They create jobs and take surplus workers off the land; they earn foreign exchange through exports and make the country self-reliant (also add value, modernise farming).

(b) Agro-based industries use farm produce as raw material, for example sugar mills; mineral-based industries use minerals, for example iron and steel plants.

(c) Public sector — owned by the government, for example the Steel Authority of India; private sector — owned by individuals or companies, for example Tata Steel; joint sector — owned by the government and private firms together; cooperative sector — owned by the producers who supply raw material, for example sugar cooperatives of Maharashtra or Amul.

(d) (i) Large-scale, mineral-based, public sector. (ii) Small-scale or cottage, agro-based, private sector. (iii) Large-scale, agro-based, cooperative sector.

questions.solution_md: Importance; agro and mineral; ownership types; three classifications.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the two leading sugar-producing states of India. [2]

(b) Name two by-products of the sugar industry and state one use of each. [2]

(c) Explain three reasons why the sugar industry has grown faster in Maharashtra and Karnataka than in the northern plains. [3]

(d) Illustrative recoveries by delay in crushing are: 0 hours 11%, 24 hours 10.5%, 48 hours 9.8%, 72 hours 9%. Calculate the sugar lost when 3000 t of cane is crushed 72 hours after cutting instead of at once, and use your answer to explain why sugar mills are located near cane fields. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra (as of the early 2020s).

(b) Bagasse — fuel for the mill’s boilers or raw material for paper; molasses — industrial alcohol (ethanol) (press mud — manure).

(c) Cane in the warm, frost-free peninsula has more sucrose and a higher yield per hectare; the crushing season is longer; well-run cooperative mills with newer machinery are common in Maharashtra.

(d) At once $= \frac{11}{100} \times 3000 = 330$ t; after 72 h $= \frac{9}{100} \times 3000 = 270$ t; loss $= 60$ t. Cane loses sucrose rapidly after cutting and is bulky to carry, so mills are built among the cane fields to crush it quickly and cheaply.

questions.solution_md: States; by-products; reasons; loss 60 t and location.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the four kinds of silk produced in India. [2]

(b) Name one centre each famous for (i) silk sarees and (ii) tasar silk. [2]

(c) Explain three reasons why Karnataka leads India in mulberry silk. [3]

(d) If about 8 kg of cocoons give 1 kg of raw silk (illustrative), how much raw silk can be reeled from 1200 kg of cocoons? Why are reeling units usually located close to the cocoon-rearing villages? [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Mulberry, tasar, eri and muga.

(b) (i) Kanchipuram (or Varanasi, Dharmavaram); (ii) Bhagalpur.

(c) An equable plateau climate lets mulberry grow all year, so five or more crops of cocoons are possible; red loamy soils and irrigation suit mulberry; long traditions, government research and support, and organised cocoon markets such as Ramanagara.

(d) Raw silk $= \frac{1200}{8} = 150$ kg. Most of the cocoon’s weight is lost in reeling, and live pupae must be killed and the cocoons reeled soon after harvest, so reeling is done near the rearing villages.

questions.solution_md: Four silks; centres; Karnataka; 150 kg.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name four factors that influence the location of an industry. [2]

(b) Why is a sugar mill pulled towards its raw material while a bakery is pulled towards its market? [2]

(c) Two illustrative sites are scored out of 10 for a sugar mill on raw material (weight 0.35), market (weight 0.2), power (weight 0.15), labour (weight 0.15), transport (weight 0.15). Site P scores 9, 5, 6, 7, 6; site Q scores 4, 9, 8, 7, 8. Calculate the weighted score of each site and choose one. [3]

(d) Site Q scored higher on market, power and transport. Explain why it still loses, and suggest one change that would make Q suitable for a different industry. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Raw material, power, labour, market (also transport, water, capital, climate, government policy).

(b) Cane is bulky and loses sucrose soon after cutting, so the mill goes to the cane; bread is perishable and needed fresh by many customers, so the bakery goes to the market.

(c) P $= 0.35 \times 9 + 0.2 \times 5 + 0.15 \times 6 + 0.15 \times 7 + 0.15 \times 6 = 7$; Q $= 0.35 \times 4 + 0.2 \times 9 + 0.15 \times 8 + 0.15 \times 7 + 0.15 \times 8 = 6.65$. Choose site P.

(d) For sugar, the raw-material factor carries the highest weight (0.35) because cane is bulky and perishable; Q’s low raw-material score (4) outweighs its other advantages. Q would suit a market-oriented industry, such as electronics assembly or food packaging for the city, for which market and transport would carry the greatest weights.

questions.solution_md: Factors; pull of raw material and market; P 7, Q 6.65; weights explain the choice.
